modules.title: The Money Map

learn.title: Five account types
learn.text: Assets are resources the business controls, including cash and customer receivables. Liabilities are obligations, including vendor bills and loans. Equity is the owner’s residual interest. Income increases equity through earned revenue; expenses decrease equity through costs. Owner investments and draws change equity without being income or expenses.

learn.title: The equation stays balanced
learn.text: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. For the live diagram, expanded equity equals owner equity + income − expenses. A loan increases cash and a liability equally. An earned invoice increases AR and income equally. Paying a previously recorded bill reduces cash and AP; the expense was already recorded with the bill.

modules.title: Double Entry Without Tears
modules.hook: A $500 entry balances perfectly, but credits Service Income for a payment on an old invoice. Balanced does not always mean correct.

learn.title: Debit and credit are sides
learn.text: Debit means the left side of an account; credit means the right. Assets and expenses normally increase with debits. Liabilities, equity and income normally increase with credits. Decreases use the opposite side. Debits and credits are not universal synonyms for money in and out: a credit to AR reduces an asset while a credit to income increases revenue.

learn.title: Two checks for every entry
learn.text: First check that total debits equal total credits. Then ask whether each account describes the actual event. An invoice debits AR and credits income. Collecting that invoice debits Checking or Undeposited Funds and credits AR. A balanced entry to the wrong account can still overstate income. QBO forms create the journals; use this builder to understand them.

learn.title: Active lab timing

modules.title: The Customer Cash Cycle
modules.hook: The bank received $500 from Oak Court. QBO shows $1,000 of income and an unpaid $500 invoice. Follow both paths to find the extra $500.

learn.title: Invoice, payment, deposit
learn.text: An invoice records earned revenue and AR. Receive Payment applies collection to that specific customer invoice. Deposit to Undeposited Funds holds receipts until you group them into the actual bank deposit. In Bank Deposit, select the held payments. A single ACH already deposited can instead be received directly to Checking, then matched; do not also create a Bank Deposit.

learn.title: Why the wrong shortcut fails
learn.text: Adding an invoiced customer receipt directly to income records the sale a second time and never clears the invoice. To repair an unreconciled mistake, inspect the invoice and Audit Log, undo the wrong feed categorization, remove the erroneous added deposit, record the proper payment and deposit, and match. Protect closed periods and get the supervisor involved before changing reconciled records.

learn.title: Active lab timing

Thirty minutes is an active-work target; use extra time for unfamiliar QBO screens.

modules.title: Bank Feeds: Match, Add, Transfer, Exclude
modules.hook: An ACH appeared, but the CRM sent no payment. The bank proves cash arrived; it does not tell you whether revenue was already invoiced.

learn.title: A feed is a queue, not the books
learn.text: A downloaded row awaits review. Match connects it to an existing entry; Add creates one. Transfer moves money between your company’s accounts. Exclude removes an irrelevant or duplicate downloaded row, not its ledger entry. Verify source documents and both accounts before excluding. Do not exclude real business activity merely because it is hard to match.

learn.title: Search before Add
learn.text: Look for the customer and open invoices, then existing payments, sales receipts and deposits. An open invoice plus confirmed ACH calls for Receive Payment applied to that invoice. This lab makes you record that payment explicitly, then choose it in Find match. QBO can offer invoice matching that creates the payment automatically; verify the application and do not receive it twice. Add to income is appropriate only for earned work with no invoice and no existing sale.

learn.title: Active lab timing
learn.text: Take six active minutes applying the decision tree to four source documents. Spend twelve practice minutes processing twelve feed rows, recording the missing payment and finding exact matches; explain each Add before submitting. Complete the seven-minute sandbox mission and three-minute check. Thirty minutes is an active-work target; use extra time for unfamiliar QBO screens.

steps.title: Is it a verified duplicate download?
steps.text: Exclude the extra feed row only; keep the genuine transaction.

steps.title: Is it a movement between company accounts?
steps.text: Use Transfer, or Match if the transfer was already recorded.

steps.title: Does a ledger record already exist?
steps.text: Find match; compare payee, amount, date and bank account.

steps.title: Is a customer invoice open?
steps.text: Receive Payment against the invoice, then Match the payment or grouped deposit.

steps.title: Is the economic event genuinely unrecorded?
steps.text: Add to the appropriate account. Income only for an unrecorded earned sale.

learn.title: Mirror the customer cycle
learn.text: A bill for supplies already used debits Supplies Expense and credits AP. Pay Bills debits AP and credits Checking. Matching the withdrawal to the saved bill payment does not create another expense. If you instead Add the withdrawal as expense, the expense is duplicated and the bill remains open.

learn.title: Bill Pay status matters
learn.text: Review vendor, bill, amount, due date, bank account and authorization. A scheduled bill payment may not yet have settled. Match the withdrawal only to the correct recorded payment; check dates and payment status if it is absent. A purchase paid immediately with no bill or existing expense can be recorded as an Expense. Buying equipment generally creates an asset, not automatically a supplies expense.

modules.title: Reconciliation
modules.hook: The statement ends at $1,303, but the cleared ledger ends at $1,339. One repair amount has transposed digits. A $36 difference is a clue, not proof.

learn.title: What reconciliation proves
learn.text: Reconcile compares the statement’s opening and ending balances with the book transactions that actually cleared. It helps prove cash completeness and accuracy; it does not prove every income or expense category is correct. Confirm account, dates, opening balance and statement ending balance first. Clear deposits and withdrawals individually against the statement. Leave outstanding checks and deposits in transit unchecked.

learn.title: Use differences as clues
learn.text: A difference equal to one transaction may mean an omitted or extra cleared item. A difference twice a transaction may indicate its sign was reversed. A difference divisible by nine may suggest transposed digits: $184 versus $148 differs by $36. None proves the cause. If the opening balance changed, inspect the reconciliation history and Audit Log for edited or deleted previously reconciled transactions. Do not plug a difference into income.

learn.title: Active lab timing
learn.text: Take six active minutes comparing statement and ledger signs. Spend twelve practice minutes checking cleared items, correcting the transposition and testing the three numerical clues against source evidence. Complete the seven-minute sandbox mission and three-minute check. Thirty minutes is an active-work target; use extra time for unfamiliar QBO screens.

steps.title: Trace clearances

modules.title: The Exceptions Lab
modules.hook: The queue is short, but every row has a hidden dependency. Diagnose the record, choose the repair, and explain what would have broken.

learn.title: Trace before repair
learn.text: Use the customer or vendor history, source documents, bank register and Audit Log. Identify the original invoice or bill, its payment and its deposit or withdrawal. Determine whether the bank download is linked. For current unreconciled mistakes, undo the incorrect categorization before removing a duplicate record and recreating the correct workflow. Verify balances after the repair.

learn.title: Protect the period and the evidence
learn.text: Do not silently rewrite reconciled or closed-period records. Ask the supervisor to choose the correction date and method. Customer refunds, credits and returned checks need linked workflows so the customer balance agrees with reality. Void keeps a zero-dollar record for supported types; delete removes the normal record but leaves Audit Log history. Document the cause and preventive check for every exception.

learn.title: Active lab timing
learn.text: Take six active minutes tracing linked records and Audit Log. Spend about one minute per exception during twelve practice minutes: state diagnosis, specific repair and economic effect before choosing an answer. Complete the seven-minute sandbox mission and three-minute check. Thirty minutes is an active-work target; use extra time for unfamiliar QBO screens.

steps.title: Diagnose
steps.text: Identify the source event, linked records, actual bank movement and affected period.

steps.title: Repair
steps.text: Correct the specific payment, deposit, application or duplicate; preserve legitimate records.

steps.title: Prove the effect
steps.text: Compare cash, AR/AP, UF, income/expense and customer/vendor detail after repair.

steps.title: Prevent recurrence
steps.text: Document the sync gap, matching check or review control that would have caught it.

practice.title: Payments stuck in holding
practice.prompt: A $750 Bank Deposit exists, but its two $500/$250 payments still sit in UF. The deposit used a new income line.

options.text: Undo the wrong feed match if necessary; replace the erroneous deposit with one selecting the two existing UF payments, then rematch
options.explanation: Correct cash remains $750. The wrong income line overstates revenue $750 and leaves UF overstated $750. Preserve the real bank deposit and review closed periods before changing it.

options.text: Receive both payments a second time
options.explanation: That would duplicate receipts and can create customer credits.

options.text: Reclassify the two UF payments as additional Service Income
options.explanation: The invoices already earned revenue and the payments already collected AR. Reclassification to income would perpetuate duplicated revenue rather than clear UF through the deposit.

practice.explanation: Correct cash remains $750. The wrong income line overstates revenue $750 and leaves UF overstated $750. Preserve the real bank deposit and review closed periods before changing it.

practice.title: Deposit bypassed the invoice
practice.prompt: A $500 ACH was added to income while its $500 invoice remains open; no payment exists.

options.text: Undo the wrong Add, remove its unreconciled duplicate-income deposit, Receive Payment against the invoice to Checking, then Match
options.explanation: Repair reduces overstated income $500 and clears overstated AR $500; the real $500 Checking receipt remains once.

options.text: Write off the unpaid invoice as bad debt
options.explanation: The customer paid. A bad-debt write-off hides the wrong collection workflow.

options.text: Receive a second payment but keep the wrong income deposit
options.explanation: Keeping both cash records duplicates Checking, while the original income error remains. Remove the erroneous added record before recording the proper workflow.

practice.explanation: Repair reduces overstated income $500 and clears overstated AR $500; the real $500 Checking receipt remains once.

practice.title: No suggested match
practice.prompt: A real $320 receipt has no suggested match, but a saved payment exists with a nearby date.

options.text: Use Find match, widen the date range, verify customer/amount/account, then match the existing payment
options.explanation: Missing suggestions are not missing bookkeeping. Adding again would overstate cash and may duplicate income or customer credit $320.

options.text: Exclude because the suggestion is missing
options.explanation: That leaves real bank activity unresolved.

options.text: Add another $320 deposit and keep the saved payment
options.explanation: That records the same bank receipt twice. Locate and match the existing payment instead.

practice.explanation: Missing suggestions are not missing bookkeeping. Adding again would overstate cash and may duplicate income or customer credit $320.

practice.title: Payment on the wrong invoice
practice.prompt: Oak Court’s $500 payment settled invoice OC-2, but remittance names OC-1. Both belong to Oak Court.

options.text: Edit the existing payment application: uncheck OC-2 and apply OC-1; verify both remaining balances
options.explanation: Cash, total AR and income stay unchanged. Invoice-level aging and collection status were wrong $500.

options.text: Create another $500 payment for OC-1
options.explanation: That overstates cash and reduces total AR a second time.

options.text: Issue a $500 credit memo to OC-1 and leave the payment on OC-2
options.explanation: The customer paid OC-1; a credit memo changes revenue/AR instead of correcting the payment allocation.

practice.explanation: Cash, total AR and income stay unchanged. Invoice-level aging and collection status were wrong $500.

practice.title: Overpayment and credit
practice.prompt: Customer pays $550 against a $500 invoice. No other sale exists.

options.text: Receive the $550, apply $500, and retain the $50 customer credit or refund it with the correct linked workflow
options.explanation: Cash increases $550; invoice AR clears $500. Remaining $50 is a customer credit, not $50 of extra earned revenue. Review unapplied-payment reporting, especially cash-basis reports.

options.text: Add the extra $50 to Service Income
options.explanation: There is no earned sale supporting that revenue.

options.text: Record only $500 received and ignore the remaining $50
options.explanation: Checking received $550. Recording only $500 understates cash and omits the customer’s $50 credit.

practice.explanation: Cash increases $550; invoice AR clears $500. Remaining $50 is a customer credit, not $50 of extra earned revenue. Review unapplied-payment reporting, especially cash-basis reports.

practice.title: Two expenses for one payment
practice.prompt: A $240 paid bill and a second added $240 expense represent one withdrawal. Neither is reconciled.

options.text: Verify the bill payment, undo the erroneous feed Add, remove the duplicate expense and match the bill payment
options.explanation: The duplicate overstates expense $240 and understates book cash $240. Removing it preserves the paid bill and correct cash.

options.text: Delete the legitimate bill payment
options.explanation: That reopens AP and preserves the wrong expense.

options.text: Keep both ledger entries but exclude the downloaded withdrawal
options.explanation: Excluding a bank download does not remove the duplicate ledger expense or repair understated book cash.

practice.explanation: The duplicate overstates expense $240 and understates book cash $240. Removing it preserves the paid bill and correct cash.

practice.title: Reconciliation difference
practice.prompt: Statement repair is −$184; ledger shows −$148. Difference is $36.

options.text: Verify the receipt and statement, correct the repair to −$184, then clear it
options.explanation: The ledger currently overstates cash $36 and understates expense $36. Nine-divisibility is a clue corroborated by source evidence.

options.text: Post a $36 income adjustment
options.explanation: A plug conceals the transaction error and misstates revenue.

options.text: Uncheck the repair and finish without recording its cleared amount
options.explanation: The repair really cleared. Omitting it does not correct the ledger’s $36 amount error or represent the statement.

practice.explanation: The ledger currently overstates cash $36 and understates expense $36. Nine-divisibility is a clue corroborated by source evidence.

practice.title: Customer refund
practice.prompt: Customer has a verified $50 overpayment credit and receives a $50 refund.

options.text: Record a $50 Expense or Check to the customer using Accounts Receivable, then use Receive Payment to link that refund to the existing overpayment credit
options.explanation: The form reduces Checking and removes the existing customer credit through AR. Linking clears the customer balance; it creates no supplies expense and no second reversal of earned revenue.

options.text: Add $50 Supplies Expense
options.explanation: The refund is settlement of a customer credit, not supplies consumed.

options.text: Record another $50 credit memo without recording the bank refund
options.explanation: A new credit increases what the customer can claim and omits the outgoing cash. The refund must settle the existing credit.

practice.explanation: The form reduces Checking and removes the existing customer credit through AR. Linking clears the customer balance; it creates no supplies expense and no second reversal of earned revenue.

practice.title: Bounced check
practice.prompt: A $400 payment already cleared an invoice, but the bank returned the check and charged a $15 fee.

options.text: Record the returned $400 withdrawal to Accounts Receivable for that customer; reapply the original payment from its invoice to the returned-payment entry; separately record the $15 Bank Fees
options.explanation: Reapplying opens the original invoice. Checking decreases $415, AR is restored $400, and bank fee expense rises $15. The earned $400 service income remains. Do not delete the original bank deposit.

options.text: Delete the invoice and exclude the withdrawal
options.explanation: The work is still earned and the real bank withdrawal needs recording.

options.text: Reduce Service Income $415 and leave the customer invoice paid
options.explanation: The $400 work remains earned and the customer owes it again. Only the separate $15 bank charge is fee expense.

practice.explanation: Reapplying opens the original invoice. Checking decreases $415, AR is restored $400, and bank fee expense rises $15. The earned $400 service income remains. Do not delete the original bank deposit.

practice.title: Void versus delete
practice.prompt: A duplicate unreconciled invoice was never valid. A separate unused check number should remain traceable.

options.text: After checking links and history, delete the duplicate invoice; void the unused check where supported to preserve its zero-dollar record
options.explanation: Deletion removes the transaction from normal records but remains in Audit Log. Void keeps a zero-dollar trace. Both change totals; neither is a safe shortcut for reconciled or closed-period entries. Some QBO types cannot be voided.

options.text: Delete every record, including reconciled checks
options.explanation: Historical changes can break prior reconciliation and remove the normal visible trace.

options.text: Void the duplicate invoice and delete the unused check number
options.explanation: Voiding can remove invoice totals, but deleting the check loses its normal visible number trace. The stated goal is to remove the accidental duplicate and preserve the unused check record.

practice.explanation: Deletion removes the transaction from normal records but remains in Audit Log. Void keeps a zero-dollar trace. Both change totals; neither is a safe shortcut for reconciled or closed-period entries. Some QBO types cannot be voided.

options.text: Total AR decreases another $100; cash is unchanged

check.title: Overpayment
check.prompt: A customer paid $50 more than invoiced. Is that automatically revenue?

options.text: No: retain or refund a customer credit
options.explanation: No additional earned work supports extra revenue.

check.title: Returned check
check.prompt: A collected $400 invoice payment bounces. What must be restored?

options.text: Customer amount due $400, with the bank reversal recorded
options.explanation: The customer still owes for earned services; a separate bank fee is expense.

options.text: Service income must be erased
options.explanation: Collection failure does not erase earned work.

options.text: Only the $15 fee; the invoice should stay paid
options.explanation: The bank took back the $400 collection too. Restore the customer amount due and record both bank movements.

check.explanation: The customer still owes for earned services; a separate bank fee is expense.

check.title: History
check.prompt: Does deleting a QBO transaction erase all evidence of it?

options.text: No: deletion remains visible in Audit Log
options.explanation: Normal records and totals change, but the audit trail retains the action.

options.text: Yes: delete erases its audit history
options.explanation: QBO retains deleted transaction history in Audit Log.

options.text: No: the deleted transaction still contributes to report totals
options.explanation: Deletion retains an Audit Log trace but removes the transaction from normal financial totals.

check.explanation: Normal records and totals change, but the audit trail retains the action.

options.explanation: A plug can hide the actual change and introduce another unsupported transaction.

options.text: Inspect the discrepancy report and transaction history against the prior statement
options.explanation: The report identifies what changed. Verify it against evidence before agreeing on a supported correction with your supervisor.

modules.title: Month-End Capstone
modules.hook: September begins with $5,000 in Checking and ends at $11,860. Process 30 imported rows, repair six exceptions, and prove the statement without a plug.

learn.title: Your evidence packet
learn.text: Opening statement balance is $5,000. The bank has 29 actual September transactions plus one duplicate import in the feed. Open invoices, paid bills and existing ledger references are listed with the rows. Six exceptions E1–E6 affect collection workflow, UF, duplicate expense, invoice application, customer credit and repair amount. Spruce Lane’s $600 invoice remains unpaid; do not invent a receipt.

learn.title: Three passes, one proof
learn.text: First process every feed row with its source evidence and exact match. Second select all six supported repairs, explaining their dollar effects. Third reconcile the statement using corrected amounts. A $90 vendor check and a $110 deposit are outstanding at month-end and must remain unchecked. The repair row begins with the incorrect ledger amount; use its source evidence to correct it. A balanced reconcile does not by itself prove invoice applications or customer credits are correct.

learn.title: Active lab timing
learn.text: Take five active minutes reading the evidence packet and planning three passes. Spend fifteen practice minutes on the thirty-row queue, six repairs and reconciliation; pause to trace dependencies instead of guessing from the amount. practice.title: Repair six linked exceptions
practice.prompt: Using the feed evidence, open invoices and existing ledger records, select all six correct repairs. Each selection addresses one distinct exception E1–E6. Reject the two shortcuts.

options.text: Receive Payment against OC-500 to Checking, then match the new payment
options.explanation: The invoice already earned revenue. Apply the actual $500 collection to AR, not income.

options.text: Replace incorrect DEP-750 with a deposit selecting MAP-500 and ELM-250 from UF, then match
options.explanation: The existing payments prove collection. Linking them in Bank Deposit clears UF without new income.

options.text: Remove the duplicate EXP-DUP-240, preserve BP-240, then match BP-240
options.explanation: One bank withdrawal belongs to one legitimate bill payment. The duplicate expense creates an extra book withdrawal.

options.text: Reapply BL-P320 from BL-2 to BL-1, then match the same payment
options.explanation: Moving the existing receipt changes which invoice is paid without changing total cash or total AR.

options.text: Match CC-P550 and retain the $50 customer credit; do not add extra revenue
options.explanation: The $550 payment clears a $500 invoice and leaves a $50 customer credit, not a second sale.

options.text: Correct EXP-REPAIR from −$148 to −$184, then clear/match that existing record
options.explanation: The $36 multiple-of-nine clue is confirmed by the $184 source receipt and statement.

options.text: Add all positive bank rows to Service Income
options.explanation: Invoices, transfers, owner investments and loans are not new earned cash sales.

options.text: Exclude unresolved rows to make reconciliation finish
options.explanation: Real bank movements need a recorded and supported workflow; exclusion hides unresolved activity.

practice.explanation: Six repairs protect different balances: receive the missing $500 against AR without repeating income; select $750 of existing UF payments so UF and duplicate income clear; remove the $240 duplicate expense to restore cash and profit; reapply $320 to the correct invoice without changing total cash or AR; retain the $50 customer credit rather than earn new revenue; correct the repair by $36, reducing cash and increasing expense. Matching links the verified records; excluding real activity fixes none of these ledger errors.
